newsitem.title: GERMANY: German equipment, plant sector sees more job cuts.
newsitem.headline: German equipment, plant sector sees more job cuts.

text.p: Germany's capital equipment and plant construction sector will cut another 10,000-20,000 jobs this year and sees tax reform as the only chance for an upturn in employment, the VDMA association said on Thursday.
The cuts mark a slowdown from last year when the sector shed 38,000 jobs or four percent of its workforce to 942,000 as new orders declined six percent.

VDMA President Michael Rogowski said the sector's prospects should brighten in the second half of the year because exports were being boosted by global economic growth and the recent depreciation of the mark against the dollar, pound and lira.
"I'm optimistic that in a year's time we'll be able to look back on 1997 and say that the mood improved significantly," Rogowski said.
The recent rise in the dollar to 1.70 marks has "put wind into the industry's sails," although a rate of 1.80 to two marks would be more justified by economic fundamentals.

But Rogowski said German industry was being weighed down by exorbitant taxes and that Germany had to follow the examples of the U.S., Britain, New Zealand and the Netherlands in carrying out radical reforms.
He noted that Britain cut its unemployment rate from 11.5 percent to 6.5 percent between 1993 and 1996 and that Germany too could halve unemployment in what he called the medium term.
"It's possible for us too, we only have to want to do it. Tax cuts would be best vitamin pill for an economic upturn."
Rogowski called on the government not to delay the implementation of proposed reforms aimed at cutting 30 billion marks off taxes.
The ruling coalition and opposition parties will meet on March 8 to try to reach a compromise on the reform package, seen as key to Bonn's efforts to boost employment and growth.
Rogowski was speaking shortly after the Federal Labour Office reported a slowdown in the rise in German unemployment in February.

Joblessness grew by 5,000 in the month to a seasonally adjusted 4.316 million after having surged by 145,000 in January. The February number is nevertheless the highest level of unemployment since Adolf Hitler came to power.
The German machine and plant construction industry's output rose just one percent last year and the VDMA has predicted output growth of three percent in 1997.
Earnings remained weak in 1996, with a return on sales of just one percent, and Rogowski predicted a slight improvement to 1.5 percent at most in 1997.
